To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

endobronchial black pigmentation in a smoker with a history of occupational inhalational anthracosis can be a manifestation of concurrent primary lung cancer, and that the presence of anthracosis should not preclude a search for primary lung cancer in patients with endobronchially visible pigmentation.

(1) a 86-year-old male with history of smoking, welding, and anthracosis was diagnosed with concurrent endobronchial pulmonary anthracosis and primary lung cancer; and (2) the patient was treated with bronchoscopic resection of endobronchially located anthracotic mass and adjuvant chemotherapy for primary lung cancer.

(1) the patient had a 4×5 cm consolidation in his RUL; (2) he had worked as a welding for 40 yrs; (3) he had a previous 10 pack-year cigarette smoking history; (4) he was asymptomatic; and (5) he was exposed to smoke and fumes without protective gear.

the study of a new method of the analysis of the data obtained from the experiments on the determination of the thermal conductivity coefficient of the gas mixture of air and helium.
the development of new methods for the determination of the composition of the organic compounds present in a complex mixture.

this case represents an incidental finding of endobronchial black pigment deposition in a 86-year-old male with no prior history of anthracosis.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of anthracotic material in the airways should not be considered as a contraindication to bronchoscopy, and that anthracosis can be a cause for bronchoscopic bleeding.
we found a significant association between anthracosis and primary lung cancer.

we have shown a novel mechanism for the development of lung cancer in the context of anthracotic pneumoconiosis and that anthracotic pneumonosis may be an important cofactor in the pathogenesis of lung cancer in smokers.
